title: Home-style mapo tofu

ingredients.note: soft or silken, cut in 2 cm cubes

steps: Simmer the tofu in salted water for 2 minutes and drain gently. This firms it and seasons it.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat and brown the beef for 3 to 4 minutes, breaking it up.
Add the doubanjiang, black beans, garlic, ginger and chilli flakes and fry for 1 to 2 minutes until the oil turns red.
Add the stock and soy sauce, bring to a simmer, and slide in the tofu. Simmer for 5 minutes, pushing gently rather than stirring.
Stir the cornstarch slurry and add in two parts, simmering until the sauce clings and turns glossy.
Finish with the ground Sichuan pepper, spring onion and chilli oil. Serve with rice.
notes: Doubanjiang is salty, so taste before adding salt. For a vegetarian version, swap the beef for mushrooms and use vegetable stock.

title: Kung pao chicken

ingredients.note: boneless thighs, cut in 2 cm pieces
white parts, cut in 2 cm lengths

steps: Mix the chicken with the marinade ingredients and leave for 15 minutes.
Stir together the sauce ingredients in a small bowl.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium heat. Add the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns and stir for 20 to 30 seconds until fragrant but not burnt.
Raise the heat, add the chicken and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes until cooked through.
Push the chicken aside and add the ginger, garlic and spring onion, stirring until fragrant, then toss everything together.
Pour in the sauce, stir for 30 seconds until glossy, then fold in the peanuts and serve at once with rice.
notes: Add the peanuts at the end to keep them crunchy. Replace the Chinkiang vinegar with rice vinegar plus a pinch of sugar if you have none.

title: Dan dan noodles
steps: Fry the pork in the oil for 5 to 6 minutes until crisp at the edges, then add the soy sauce and Shaoxing wine and cook until dry. Set aside.
Divide the sesame paste, soy sauce, chilli oil, vinegar, sugar, garlic and Sichuan pepper between two bowls and loosen each with the hot stock.
Boil the noodles until just tender, adding the pak choi for the last minute. Drain well.
Place the noodles in the bowls, top with the pork, pak choi, peanuts and spring onion, and toss thoroughly before eating.
notes: Add a spoon of preserved mustard stem (ya cai) to the topping if you have it. Loosen the sauce with a little noodle water if too thick.

title: Quick Sichuan paocai
steps: Dissolve the salt and sugar in the cooled water in a very clean jar or crock.
Add the ginger, garlic, Sichuan pepper, chillies and star anise.
Pack in the vegetables so they are fully under the brine, pressing down with a weight or a small plate if needed.
Close the lid loosely, leaving some room for gas, and keep at room temperature for 2 to 3 days until pleasantly sour.
Refrigerate and eat within 2 weeks. Top up the brine with more vegetables for a new batch.
notes: Use only clean utensils; scum or off smells mean the batch should be discarded. Rinse and eat as a side with rice or noodles, or add to stir-fries.

title: Har gow
steps: Mix the shrimp, bamboo shoots, lard, sesame oil, sugar, pepper, cornstarch and salt. Stir in one direction for 1 minute and chill for 30 minutes.
Mix the two starches with a pinch of salt in a bowl. Pour in the boiling water and stir at once with chopsticks into a rough dough, then cover for 5 minutes.
Add the oil and knead the warm dough until smooth. Keep it covered while you work.
Divide into 16 small balls. Flatten each ball between oiled parchment, with a cleaver or a small pan, to a thin round about 7 cm across.
Place a teaspoon of filling in the centre, fold over and pleat the edge in small folds, pressing it shut.
Steam the dumplings on parchment in a steamer over boiling water for 6 to 7 minutes until translucent. Serve with soy sauce.
notes: The dough dries quickly and must stay covered. Do not overfill, or the wrapper will tear.

title: Home-oven char siu

ingredients.note: boneless shoulder, cut lengthwise into 4 cm strips

steps: Mix all marinade ingredients, coat the pork and marinate in the fridge for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight.
Heat the oven to 220 C. Set the pork on a rack over a tray with a little water in the tray to prevent burning.
Roast for 20 minutes, then brush with some leftover marinade and turn. Roast for 15 minutes more.
Brush with the honey glaze and roast for 5 to 8 minutes until charred at the edges and the thickest piece reaches at least 70 C inside.
Rest for 10 minutes, slice across the grain and serve over rice or with noodles.
notes: Shoulder is best because it stays moist. Boil any leftover marinade for 3 minutes before using it as a sauce.

title: Dongpo pork
steps: Blanch the whole pork belly in boiling water for 5 minutes. Drain, rinse and cut into 5 cm squares.
Line the bottom of a heavy pot with the spring onions and ginger. Lay the pork on top, skin side down.
Add the wine, both soy sauces, sugar, star anise and water. The liquid should come about two thirds up the meat.
Bring to a boil, cover tightly, and cook on the lowest heat for 2 hours, turning once, until a chopstick slides through easily.
Uncover, lift out the pork and reduce the sauce over high heat for 5 to 10 minutes to a glossy glaze.
Return the pork, skin side up, and spoon the sauce over. Serve with rice and steamed greens.
notes: It is rich, so serve small portions. It reheats well and tastes better the next day.

title: Pork and cabbage jiaozi

ingredients.note: finely chopped, salted and squeezed dry

steps: Mix the flour and water to a firm dough, knead for 8 minutes until smooth, cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the pork with the soy sauce, wine, ginger, pepper and 2 tbsp water by stirring one way for 2 minutes. Fold in the cabbage, spring onion and sesame oil.
Roll the dough into a rope and cut it into about 40 pieces. Roll each to a thin round about 8 cm wide.
Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in each round, fold over and pinch with a few pleats to seal.
Boil in plenty of water for 5 to 6 minutes, until they float and the filling is cooked, and serve with the vinegar and soy dip.
notes: To pan-fry, fry in a little oil until golden, add 100 ml water, cover and steam for 6 minutes. Freeze uncooked dumplings on a tray, then bag, and boil from frozen for 8 minutes.

title: Xinjiang-style lamb skewers

ingredients.note: shoulder or leg with some fat, cut in 2 cm cubes

steps: Mix the lamb with the grated onion, oil and half the salt, and marinate for 1 hour. Soak wooden skewers in water for 30 minutes.
Thread the lamb onto skewers, packing the pieces closely.
Grill over hot charcoal or under a very hot grill for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until browned and cooked through.
Mix the cumin, chilli flakes, pepper and remaining salt and sprinkle generously over the skewers while hot. Serve with flatbread.
notes: Leave the lamb fat on; it keeps the meat moist and carries the cumin.

title: Cantonese brown sugar nian gao
steps: Warm the sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, then cool to room temperature.
Whisk the sugar syrup into the flour a little at a time until a smooth, lump-free batter forms. Stir in the oil.
Oil a 18 cm round tin and line the base with parchment. Pour in the batter.
Cover loosely with foil and steam over boiling water for 50 to 60 minutes, until the cake is firm and glossy and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool completely before cutting, since the cake is too sticky to cut while warm. Serve as is, or pan-fry slices until crisp outside and soft inside.
notes: Keep refilling the steamer with hot water. The cake keeps for several days in the fridge and firms up when cold, so steam or fry it before eating.
